[[File:Apollonius quadrilateral.svg|thumb|180px|An example of an Apollonius quadrilateral]]

In [[geometry]], an '''Apollonius quadrilateral''' is a [[quadrilateral]] <math>ABCD</math> such that the two products of opposite side lengths are equal. That is,{{r|harras}}
<math display=block>\overline{AB}\cdot\overline{CD}=\overline{AD}\cdot\overline{BC}.</math>
An equivalent way of stating this definition is that the [[cross ratio]] of the four points is <math>\pm 1</math>.{{r|beamin}} It is allowed for the quadrilateral sides to cross.{{r|harras}}

The Apollonius quadrilaterals are important in [[inversive geometry]], because the property of being an Apollonius quadrilateral is preserved by [[Möbius transformation]]s, and every continuous transformation of the plane that preserves all Apollonius quadrilaterals must be a Möbius transformation.{{r|harras}}

Every [[kite (geometry)|kite]] is an Apollonius quadrilateral. A special case of the Apollonius quadrilaterals are the [[harmonic quadrilateral]]s; these are [[Cyclic quadrilateral|cyclic]] Apollonius quadrilaterals, inscribed in a given [[circle]]. They may be constructed by choosing two opposite vertices <math>A</math> and <math>C</math> arbitrarily on the circle, letting <math>E</math> be any point exterior to the circle on line <math>AC</math>, and setting <math>B</math> and <math>D</math> to be the two points where the circle is touched by the [[tangent lines to circles]] through <math>E</math>. Then <math>ABCD</math> is an Apollonius quadrilateral.{{r|harras}}

If <math>A</math>, <math>B</math>, and <math>C</math> are fixed, then the [[locus (geometry)|locus]] of points <math>D</math> that form an Apollonius quadrilateral <math>ABCD</math> is the set of points where the ratio of distances to <math>A</math> and <math>C</math>, <math>\overline{AD}/\overline{CD}</math>, is the fixed ratio <math>\overline{AB}/\overline{BC}</math>; this is just a rewritten form of the defining equation for an Apollonius quadrilateral.{{r|harras}} As [[Apollonius of Perga]] proved, the set of points <math>D</math> having a fixed ratio of distances to two given points <math>A</math> and <math>C</math>, and therefore the locus of points that form an Apollonius quadrilateral, is a circle in a family of circles called the [[Apollonian circles]]. Because <math>B</math> defines the same ratio of distances, it lies on the same circle. In the case where the fixed ratio is one, the circle [[degeneracy (mathematics)|degenerates]] to a line, the [[perpendicular bisector]] of <math>AC</math>, and the resulting quadrilateral is a kite.{{r|harras}}
